items.label: Helvetic Republic: French intervention and imposed constitution
items.meaning: French conquest of northern Italy made Swiss Alpine communications strategically important. Ochs sought a unitary state partly to resist domination by France or Austria, while La Harpe promoted Vaud’s liberation from Berne; these aims were not identical with consent to a Swiss-wide settlement. French intervention against Berne and local resistance produced an imposed Helvetic constitution without national ratification or broad cantonal consent. French forces impounded city treasuries; the treaty of 2 August granted France perpetual access to the Alpine passes and ensured continuing French military presence, reversing the reformers’ hope of protection from external domination. Ochs and La Harpe sought limits on requisitions, and Ochs later supported a French militia demand that the legislature rejected; reformers’ influence did not ensure either restraint by France or domestic consent. Ochs drafted the unitary constitution in Paris with French collaborators; annexation of Mulhouse and Geneva was intended to signal local revolt.

items.label: Bonaparte and the political management of occupied Italy
items.meaning: Bonaparte's use of Italian patriots, suppression of independent radicalism, creation of client institutions, and priority for strategic and fiscal goals. The Directory initially intended to occupy and exploit Italy as a bargaining counter for the Rhineland; Bonaparte’s early disregard of the Alba republic and later selective republicanization likewise lacked a settled liberation blueprint. Extraction included artworks and remittances to France, while Pavia’s revolt met punitive sack. Conservative Cispadane electoral success helped prompt amalgamation into the Cisalpine Republic, whose first officeholders Bonaparte nominated. Bonaparte left the Alba rebels to the defeated Piedmontese king; the Directory’s distrust of radical Italian exiles increased through their association with the Babeuf plot.

items.label: Bonaparte's religious policy and the road to reconciliation with Rome
items.meaning: Bonaparte recognized religion’s political power and used reconciliation with the Church to stabilize France. Popular Catholic observance revived after 1795 despite official anticlericalism; revolutionary religious reorganization had left a deep, persistent domestic wound. Pius VI’s death in captivity prompted mistaken Parisian predictions of papal extinction, while the Venetian conclave and election of the pragmatic Pius VII opened a path to negotiation. Bonaparte’s instrumental approach included displaying adherence to Islam in Egypt and advising gradual treatment of religion like property. Quiet relaxation of compulsory décadi observance in favor of Sunday prepared reconciliation, publicly celebrated at the Easter 1802 mass in Notre-Dame. Negotiations faced foot-dragging from ministers including Talleyrand, an apostate former bishop, and Fouché, a priest turned dechristianizer.

items.label: Nobility: loss of privilege and social transformation
items.meaning: The Revolution ended noble corporate status, feudal and fiscal privilege, venal ennoblement and automatic deference. Emigration, confiscation, execution and failed return caused trauma, but property recovery and later elite continuity limit any claim of total material destruction. Napoleon created a new nobility and incorporated surviving old nobles who could demonstrate landed wealth, an accommodation distinct from restoring their former corporate privileges or undoing emigrant losses. The Society of Thirty deliberately exploited divisions within the educated elite to mobilize support for an undivided legislature, helping convert a reform-minded order into a presumed enemy. items.label: Women: political participation and exclusion from equal rights
items.meaning: Women played decisive roles in journées, religious resistance, salons, clubs, and political writing but were excluded from equal political rights and confined ideologically to domestic roles. Nuns formed a cohesive center of resistance to the clerical oath, and lay women helped lead the late-1790s return to Catholic observance. Conflict between revolutionary clubwomen and market women accompanied the Convention’s ban on women’s organizations on 30 October 1793, a specific exclusion distinct from the Code’s later property restrictions. Théroigne de Méricourt and Claire Lacombe exemplified distinct militant roles. required_access_facets.meaning: Women played decisive roles in journées, religious resistance, salons, clubs, and political writing but were excluded from equal political rights and confined ideologically to domestic roles. Nuns formed a cohesive center of resistance to the clerical oath, and lay women helped lead the late-1790s return to Catholic observance. Conflict between revolutionary clubwomen and market women accompanied the Convention’s ban on women’s organizations on 30 October 1793, a specific exclusion distinct from the Code’s later property restrictions. Théroigne de Méricourt and Claire Lacombe exemplified distinct militant roles. Olympe de Gouges asserted equal political rights, attacked Robespierre, offered to defend the king and was arrested after demanding plebiscitary government; her execution does not establish that women’s-rights advocacy itself was the charge.

items.label: Right of resistance, Babeuf, and the modern idea of revolution
items.meaning: Declarations of a right to resist oppression legitimized insurrection, while Babeuf and later self-conscious revolutionaries made planned social revolution a reproducible political project. Babeuf used the declarations’ right of resistance to pursue material equality beyond the property-protecting equality accepted by governing constitutions. Because later regimes traced their title to the nation’s extra-legal seizure of sovereignty in 1789, revolutionaries could not simply deny resistance’s legitimacy. The overthrow of monarchy in August 1792 was presented as a second revolution exercising that right, a precedent for later claimed resistance.

items.label: The French Revolution as modern archetype and cultural tragedy
items.meaning: The Revolution became a model of deliberate political transformation and altered political culture, memory and imagined human agency. The author’s final assessment weighs courage and Enlightenment idealism against institutional destruction, mass death, and ruined lives in France and abroad. Its horrifying novelty included systematic governmental execution over months in a country celebrated for civilization and humane Enlightenment, distinct from the already familiar phenomenon of massacre. Its founders failed to see that reason and benevolent intention alone could not safely replace accumulated institutional experience; the generation living through the next twenty-six years bore the costs of resulting mistakes.

items.label: Toussaint L'Ouverture, restored slavery, and Haitian independence
items.meaning: Toussaint’s switch to the Republic and formerly enslaved troops drove out Spanish forces and established black military power, including violent punishment of collaborating whites and persecution of free people of colour. British intervention ended in withdrawal after devastating climate and disease losses, a separate failure. Toussaint was formally French-loyal but autonomous. Bonaparte’s reconquest captured him, yet disease, resistance renewed after news of slavery’s restoration, and renewed Anglo-French war defeated French control. Slavery was not re-established in Saint-Domingue; Haiti declared independence in 1804, followed by Dessalines’s imperial claim and another massacre of whites.
